title: English for Academic Purposes — Advanced Writing

points.sub: A distinct register, not just formal
pts: Academic writing has its own conventions beyond general formality — hedged claims, explicit argumentation structure, citation practices.
Treating 'academic' as simply 'more formal' underprepares learners for its genuinely distinct demands.
This builds directly on Unit 33's genre awareness, applied to one of the most demanding genre families learners will encounter.
points.who: John Swales's work on academic discourse

v: Three short texts on the same topic (written for this book)

items: Give learners three short texts on the same topic: a WhatsApp message, a newspaper paragraph and an academic paragraph.
In pairs, learners rank them from least to most academic and list the features that led to their ranking.
Collect features on the board under four headings: vocabulary, grammar, stance and sources.
Conclude together that formality is one feature of academic writing, but that stance, argument and citation are what make it distinct.
Learners bring a paragraph from their own subject textbook (in English or their home language) and analyse it using the four headings.
Support: provide a checklist of features to tick for each text.
Challenge: learners rewrite the newspaper paragraph as an academic paragraph and justify each change.

blocks.x: Three texts on the same topic (written for this book):

lines: WhatsApp: Too many kids in Bengaluru buses are glued to their phones!!
Newspaper: City commuters, especially teenagers, now spend most of their journey on mobile phones, a survey shows.
Academic: Survey data from 412 urban commuters suggest that adolescents may spend a substantially greater proportion of travel time on mobile devices than adults (Rao 2022).
T: The newspaper is formal. So why isn’t it academic?
S1: No reference.
S2: And it says ‘shows’. The third one says ‘suggest’ and ‘may’.
T: Exactly. The academic writer tells us how sure she is, and where the evidence comes from.

body: Purpose: to show that academic writing adds features beyond formality. Content: a staircase of three steps labelled ‘informal’, ‘formal’ and ‘academic’; the top step carries three extra icons (a balance scale for stance, a chain for argument, quotation marks for sources). Style: clean, minimal. Board version: three steps with the icons as simple symbols.

items: Manchester Academic Phrasebank (free, University of Manchester) for examples of academic phrasing by function.

blocks.x: Photocopied or board-written texts and a four-column table in notebooks.

pts: Academic argument typically requires not just a claim and evidence, but explicit engagement with counter-arguments and limitations.
This is a more demanding structure than Unit 39's spoken-debate argument pattern, requiring more explicit hedging and nuance.
Explicit teaching of this structure, with move analysis (Unit 54), makes an often-implicit convention learnable.

v: A model argumentative paragraph or short essay (written for this book); coloured pens

items: Introduce the four moves: claim, evidence, counter-argument (or limitation), and response (rebuttal or concession).
Learners read a model paragraph and underline each move in a different colour.
Contrast this structure with the spoken debate pattern of Unit 39: in writing, the counter-argument must be stated fairly and answered explicitly.
Learners write their own paragraph on a given claim, using the four moves, and label them in the margin.
Use Toulmin’s (1958) terms (claim, data, warrant, qualifier, rebuttal) with learners from law, philosophy or science backgrounds.
Support: give sentence frames for each move.
Challenge: learners add a qualifier that limits the scope of the claim.

blocks.x: A model paragraph with its moves labelled (written for this book):

lines: Claim: Mother-tongue instruction in the early years appears to support later achievement in English.
Evidence: Several longitudinal studies report that children who first learned to read in their home language later outperformed peers in second-language literacy.
Counter-argument: Critics argue that such findings may reflect family background rather than the language of instruction.
Response: While this concern is valid, studies that control for socio-economic status report similar patterns, although the effect is smaller.

body: Purpose: to show academic argument as a sequence of moves. Content: four linked boxes in a row (claim, evidence, counter-argument, response), with an arrow looping back from ‘response’ to ‘claim’ labelled ‘refined claim’. Style: diagrammatic, with labels in addition to colours. Board version: four boxes and a looping arrow.

items: Google Docs (free) with the highlight tool for colour-coding moves.

blocks.x: Coloured pens, or different underlining styles.

pts: Academic writing uses hedging language ('may suggest,' 'appears to') to calibrate claim strength appropriately to the evidence.
This extends Unit 53's hedging and mitigation work into its most demanding, convention-bound genre context.
Under-hedged academic writing can read as overconfident or naive to an academic audience; over-hedged writing can seem evasive.

v: Claim cards; a line on the board from ‘certain’ to ‘possible’

items: Draw a cline on the board: ‘possible’ at one end, ‘certain’ at the other.
Give groups cards with the same claim expressed with different strengths (see model language).
Groups place the cards along the cline and justify the order.
Describe the evidence (one small survey; three large studies) and ask which claim each justifies.
Learners revise an over-confident sentence and an over-hedged one from their own drafts.
Link to Unit 53: compare academic hedging with mitigation in polite spoken requests.
Support: limit the set to four cards.
Challenge: learners find three hedges and two boosters in a real article from their field and explain each choice.

lines: Mobile phone use causes poor sleep in adolescents.
Mobile phone use is associated with poorer sleep in adolescents.
Mobile phone use may contribute to poorer sleep in some adolescents.
It is possible that mobile phone use plays some role in sleep quality.
T: You have one survey of 60 students in one college. Which card can you defend?
S1: The third one. ‘May contribute’, ‘some’.

blocks.x: Under-hedging reads as naive to an academic reader; over-hedging reads as evasive. The target is a claim that matches the evidence (Hyland 1998).

body: Purpose: to show hedging as calibration. Content: a horizontal slider from ‘possible’ to ‘certain’, with claim cards placed along it; beneath, stacks of paper of different heights labelled ‘evidence’ align with each card. Style: clear infographic. Board version: a line with four marked points and short phrases.

items: AntConc (free) to search a small set of articles for may, suggest, clearly and demonstrate.

blocks.x: Claim cards on paper slips and a chalk line on the board.

pts: Citation conventions vary by discipline and style guide, but the underlying principle — crediting and engaging with sources — is universal to academic writing.
Teach citation as a genuine rhetorical skill (situating one's argument relative to others), not just a mechanical formatting requirement.
This connects to intercultural awareness (Unit 24) — citation norms and their cultural framing vary across educational traditions.

v: Three short source summaries (written for this book); reporting-verb cards

items: Present three short summaries of sources that take different positions on a question.
Contrast integral (Rao (2022) argues…) and non-integral (… (Rao 2022)) citation, and what each foregrounds.
Sort reporting verbs by stance: neutral (states, reports), positive (demonstrates, shows), and distancing (claims, asserts).
Learners write a paragraph that positions their own view in relation to all three sources.
Discuss academic integrity: what counts as using a source well, and why paraphrase and quotation must be acknowledged.
Compare how sources are acknowledged in learners’ home-language academic writing (Unit 24).
Support: provide reporting-verb cards with example sentences.
Challenge: learners identify the ‘niche’ their paragraph occupies, using Swales’s (1990) CARS model.

blocks.x: Positioning a view in relation to others (written for this book):

lines: Rao (2022) reports a strong link between phone use and poor sleep, while Iyer (2023) finds the effect largely disappears once study hours are controlled. Building on Iyer’s approach, this essay argues that…
T: Why did the writer choose ‘reports’ for Rao, not ‘claims’?
S1: ‘Claims’ would mean she doesn’t believe Rao.
T: Yes. Your reporting verb is part of your argument.

blocks.x: The names are fictional. Pennycook (1996) reminds teachers that ideas about textual ownership are culturally shaped; copying may reflect different norms rather than an intent to cheat.

body: Purpose: to present citation as rhetorical positioning. Content: a round table with three seated figures labelled with source names and speech bubbles; a fourth figure, the student writer, pulls up a chair and speaks, with arrows showing agreement and disagreement. Style: warm, human. Board version: four stick figures around a circle.

items: Zotero (free, open source) for managing sources and generating citations in different styles.

blocks.x: A handwritten source log: author, year, main claim, page, ‘my response’.

pts: Academic English favours nominalisation (turning verbs into nouns: 'analyse' becomes 'analysis') at a higher rate than conversational English.
This grammatical shift is a genuine register marker, teachable explicitly rather than left to accumulate through exposure alone.
Corpus evidence (Unit 58) can concretely demonstrate this pattern's frequency in real academic texts.

v: Pairs of sentences (written for this book); a concordance printout or screen

items: Show a spoken-style sentence and its nominalized academic equivalent (see model language).
Learners identify what has changed: which verbs became nouns, and what happened to the people doing the action.
Show a concordance of analysis of or the development of from an academic corpus (Unit 58).
Learners nominalize three sentences and discuss what is gained (density, linking) and lost (who did what).
Learners edit one paragraph of their own draft, deciding where nominalization helps and where it obscures.
For science students, work with lab reports; for social science students, with policy summaries.
Support: a table of common verb–noun pairs (analyse/analysis, decide/decision, increase/increase).
Challenge: learners track how a nominal at the end of one sentence becomes the theme of the next.

blocks.x: From spoken to academic (written for this book):

lines: Spoken: Because the teachers changed how they assessed the students, the students did better.
Academic: Changes in assessment practice led to improved student performance.
Next sentence: This improvement was most marked among first-generation learners.
T: What did ‘did better’ become?
Ss: ‘Improved performance’.
T: And in the next sentence it becomes ‘this improvement’. The noun lets the writer carry the idea forward.

body: Purpose: to show nominalization as compression. Content: a long clause shown as a string of loose beads, then packed into a single labelled box (‘improved performance’) that is passed to the next sentence like a parcel. Style: simple, metaphorical. Board version: a long line of words, an arrow, and a boxed noun phrase.

items: AntConc (free) for a teacher-built corpus of articles.

blocks.x: A printed concordance sheet of 20 lines prepared in advance.

pts: Academic writing typically demands more extended drafting and revision than other genres, given its argumentative complexity.
This extends Unit 3's process-writing introduction into a genuinely extended, multi-draft practice appropriate to this genre's demands.
Peer review at this level (Unit 43) benefits from discipline-specific or genre-specific feedback criteria.

v: A writing task; a genre-specific peer review sheet

items: Draft 1 (ideas): learners write a rough argument, focusing only on claim and evidence.
Peer review 1: partners use questions about argument only (see model language). No grammar comments at this stage.
Draft 2 (structure and stance): learners add the counter-argument, response, citations and hedges.
Peer review 2: partners check move structure, hedging and citation.
Draft 3 (language): learners edit for grammar, nominalization and cohesion (Unit 52), then submit with a short note on what changed.
Learners from the same discipline form review groups so that feedback reflects their field’s conventions (Unit 43).
Support: shorter texts and a model of each draft stage.
Challenge: learners write a reflective cover letter explaining how they responded to each comment.

blocks.x: Peer review questions, stage 1 and stage 2:

lines: What is the writer’s main claim? Write it in one sentence.
Which piece of evidence is strongest? Which is weakest?
Is there a counter-argument? Is it stated fairly?
Find one claim that is too strong for its evidence.
A: Your claim is clear, but you only have one study.
B: So I should say ‘may’?
A: Or find another study. Either change the claim or change the evidence.

blocks.x: This extends the process writing of Unit 3 into a longer, more demanding cycle.

body: Purpose: to show an extended drafting process. Content: three stacked pages labelled ‘ideas’, ‘structure and stance’, ‘language’, each with a small magnifying glass showing what the reviewer looks for. Style: tidy, sequential. Board version: three rectangles with labels and arrows.

items: Google Docs (free) with comments and version history for tracking changes between drafts.

blocks.x: Drafts on paper with peer comments on sticky notes or in a separate column.

body: Keep grammar out of the first peer review. When learners see red marks on sentence errors, they fix the surface and leave the argument untouched.

pts: General EAP teaches broadly transferable academic writing skills; discipline-specific EAP (English for Specific Academic Purposes) targets a particular field's conventions.
This connects to Unit 65's ESP course design principles, applied specifically to the academic writing domain.
Choose based on learner population — a mixed-discipline group typically needs general EAP; a single-discipline cohort can go more specific.

v: Learner profile data; a needs questionnaire (Unit 2)

items: List the disciplines, levels and writing tasks of your learners (for example, B.Sc. nursing assignments, M.A. history essays, engineering project reports).
Decide whether the group shares one discipline, a family of disciplines, or many.
Map common elements (argument, hedging, citation) and discipline-specific elements (lab report format, case study structure).
Choose a model: general EAP, discipline-specific EAP, or a general core with discipline-specific strands.
Identify one subject lecturer you could consult about real assignments (Unit 55).
In a DIET or college setting, run this as a workshop with teacher educators who teach research methods to B.Ed. or M.Ed. students.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: A first-year English-medium college class with commerce, science and arts students: general EAP core (argument, hedging, citation, summary), with optional tasks from each field.
An M.Sc. nursing cohort: discipline-specific EAP built around care plans, case reports and research proposals, planned with a nursing lecturer.

blocks.x: A mixed group needs transferable skills; a single-discipline group can go further into its field’s genres (Hyland 2006).

body: Purpose: to show EAP course types. Content: a dial between ‘general EAP’ and ‘specific EAP’, with three learner groups placed along it and a small tree diagram showing a shared trunk (general skills) branching into disciplines. Style: clean. Board version: a line with three marked points.

items: Google Forms (free) for a short writing-needs survey.

blocks.x: A paper needs questionnaire and a tally on chart paper.

pts: An academic writing rubric should assess argumentation structure and hedging appropriateness, not just grammar and organisation generically.
This connects to Unit 46's task-specific rubric principle, applied to academic writing's particular, demanding conventions.
Share genuine academic writing samples as calibration benchmarks for both teachers and learners assessing this genre.

v: Four learner essays (anonymized, with consent); a draft rubric

items: Draft a rubric with five criteria: argument structure, use of evidence and sources, stance and hedging, academic style (including nominalization), and accuracy.
Weight the criteria so that argument and sources carry more than accuracy (Unit 46).
With colleagues, score four essays independently.
Compare scores and agree benchmark essays for each band.
Share the rubric and one benchmark essay with learners before their next task.
Invite a subject lecturer to score one essay with you, to see whether your criteria match the discipline’s expectations.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Band descriptors for ‘stance and hedging’ (written for this book):

lines: 4: Claims are consistently matched to evidence; hedges and boosters are chosen deliberately.
3: Most claims are appropriately qualified; one or two are over- or under-stated.
2: Claims are often stated as facts regardless of evidence, or hedged so heavily that the position is unclear.
A: I gave this essay 4 for accuracy but only 2 for stance.
B: Same. Beautiful English, but everything is ‘proves’ and ‘clearly’.
A: That is exactly what a grammar-only rubric would miss.

body: Purpose: to show a genre-appropriate rubric. Content: a five-row rubric grid; the rows for argument, sources and stance are wider (heavier weight) than accuracy. Style: tidy table with weight bars. Board version: five rows with weights in the margin.

items: Google Sheets (free) for comparing scores across raters.
Turnitin or DrillBit (institutional licences) for similarity reports, used to open a conversation rather than to deliver a verdict.

blocks.x: Photocopied essays and a paper scoring grid.

body: Take one essay a learner has already written. Mark it twice: once with your usual scheme, once with the five-criterion academic rubric. If the two grades differ by a whole band, share both with the learner and ask which feedback helps more.

dek: Unit 61 of 100: the specific demands of academic writing — argumentation, citation, hedging, and register — for learners headed toward higher education or research.

aims.x: This unit is for teachers of advanced learners who are heading towards undergraduate study, postgraduate research, or professional work that involves reports and proposals. It treats academic writing not as ‘formal English’ but as a distinct family of genres, with its own ways of arguing, qualifying claims, using sources and packaging information in grammar.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: explain why academic writing is a distinct register and not simply a more formal version of general English;
teach the claim–evidence–counter-argument–rebuttal structure of academic argument through move analysis;
help learners calibrate claim strength with hedges and boosters appropriate to their evidence;
teach citation as a rhetorical act of positioning, and discuss academic integrity without treating learners as suspects;
raise awareness of nominalization and use corpus evidence to show how it works;
manage an extended, multi-draft writing process with genre-specific peer review;
decide between general and discipline-specific EAP for a given learner group;
design and calibrate a rubric that assesses academic argument, hedging and source use.

why: Why this matters. General C1 writing competence doesn't automatically transfer to academic writing's particular conventions. EAP is its own specialised teaching domain.

background.x: English for Academic Purposes (EAP) grew out of the wider ESP movement of the 1970s and 1980s (Unit 65), and its most influential idea came from John Swales (1990): academic texts belong to genres, recognized by a discourse community, and each genre is built from a sequence of rhetorical moves. His ‘Create a Research Space’ (CARS) model of research article introductions showed that expert writers do three predictable things: establish a territory, identify a niche, and occupy it. This unit therefore builds on the genre awareness of Unit 33 and the teaching cycle of Unit 54.

Ken Hyland’s work (1998, 2006) added a second insight: academic writing is interactive. Writers constantly signal how confident they are, how they relate to other researchers, and what they expect readers to accept. Hedges (may, appears to, suggests) and boosters (clearly, demonstrates) are not decoration; they are how a writer takes responsibility for a claim. Grammar matters too. Corpus-based descriptions such as the Longman Grammar of Spoken and Written English (Biber et al. 1999) show that academic prose is dense with nouns and noun phrases, and M. A. K. Halliday’s account of grammatical metaphor explains why: turning processes into things (analyse → analysis) allows a writer to pack information and build argument across sentences (Halliday and Martin 1993).

Many Indian learners move from regional-medium or state-board schooling into colleges and research programmes where every assignment and thesis is in English. The University Grants Commission’s 2018 regulations on academic integrity and plagiarism have made source use a formal institutional concern [VERIFY exact title and year of the UGC regulations]. At the same time, NEP 2020 encourages bilingual teaching and research in Indian languages (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020), and NCF 2023 frames languages as resources for thinking (NCERT 2023). EAP teachers can honour both: learners’ home-language academic traditions, including Kannada, Hindi or Tamil scholarly prose, are a basis for comparison, not an obstacle.

items: Move analysis. Learners label the moves in an unseen argumentative paragraph from their own field.
Hedging revision. Learners revise three over- or under-stated claims and justify each change with reference to the evidence.
Source synthesis. A paragraph that integrates three sources with deliberate reporting-verb choices and correct citation.
Portfolio of drafts. Three drafts of one essay with peer comments and a short reflection on what changed and why.
When you teach ‘academic writing’, how much of your time goes on formality and how much on argument and stance?
How do you respond when a learner submits work with unacknowledged copying? Is your response educational or only punitive?
How could learners’ home-language academic traditions become a point of comparison in your class?
What does your current rubric reward most in academic writing?

reading: Biber, D., S. Johansson, G. Leech, S. Conrad, and E. Finegan. 1999. Longman Grammar of Spoken and Written English. Harlow: Pearson Education.
Halliday, M. A. K. and J. R. Martin. 1993. Writing Science: Literacy and Discursive Power. London: Falmer Press.
Hyland, K. 1998. Hedging in Scientific Research Articles. Amsterdam: John Benjamins.
Hyland, K. 2006. English for Academic Purposes: An Advanced Resource Book. London: Routledge.
Ministry of Human Resource Development. 2020. National Education Policy 2020. New Delhi: Government of India.
NCERT. 2023. National Curriculum Framework for School Education 2023. New Delhi: National Council of Educational Research and Training.
Pennycook, A. 1996. ‘Borrowing others’ words: text, ownership, memory, and plagiarism’. TESOL Quarterly 30/2: 201–30.
Swales, J. M. 1990. Genre Analysis: English in Academic and Research Settings. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.
Toulmin, S. 1958. The Uses of Argument. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.
perm: All model texts, claims, rubrics and dialogues are original and written for this book; named sources in sample paragraphs (Rao, Iyer) are fictional and must be labelled so for learners. Screenshots of Zotero, Google Docs, AntConc, Turnitin or DrillBit require permission or replacement with original illustrations. Extracts from published articles used for analysis must be short, acknowledged and within fair dealing. Learner essays used as benchmarks need written consent and anonymization.

terms.def: A word or phrase that expresses a writer’s certainty about a claim, such as clearly or demonstrates; with hedges, boosters help writers calibrate claim strength in academic writing.
Swales’s (1990) model of how research article introductions establish a territory, identify a gap and occupy the gap; often abbreviated CARS.
A group that shares goals, genres and specialized language, such as nurses, engineers or academic researchers, and recognizes what counts as a good text in its field (Swales 1990).

Teaching English for study in further and higher education, focusing on academic genres, reading, listening to lectures, citation and argument. It developed out of the wider English for Specific Purposes movement.

Expressing a meaning in a less direct grammatical form, especially turning processes into nouns, as in analyse becoming analysis (Halliday and Martin 1993). It makes academic writing dense and abstract.
Using language to soften a claim or show caution, such as may, seems, perhaps or it could be argued. It is important in academic writing and in polite disagreement.
A citation in which the author’s name is part of the sentence, as in ‘Rao (2022) argues…’, as opposed to non-integral citation, where the name appears only in brackets (Swales 1990).
Identifying the sequence of moves in texts of a genre and the language typically used to realize each move (Swales 1990); it gives learners a map for reading and writing that genre.
Expressing processes or qualities as nouns, as in the evaporation of water instead of water evaporates; it is a key feature of academic and scientific writing that learners need to recognize and use.

A verb used to introduce or attribute the words or ideas of others, such as argue, claim, suggest or note. In academic writing, the choice of reporting verb signals the writer’s stance towards the source.

61.1.alt: Three steps rise from informal to formal to academic, and the academic step adds stance, argument and sources.

61.2.alt: Four moves in a row, claim, evidence, counter-argument and response, with a loop back to a refined claim.

61.3.alt: A scale from possible to certain on which claims are placed according to how much evidence supports them.

61.4.alt: The student writer at the centre of a conversation with three sources, agreeing with some and disagreeing with others.

61.5.alt: A long clause is packed into the noun phrase ‘improved performance’, which is passed to the next sentence.

61.6.alt: Three drafts in sequence, focusing first on ideas, then on structure and stance, then on language.

61.7.alt: A shared trunk of general academic skills branching into specific disciplines.

61.8.alt: A rubric in which argument, sources and stance carry heavier weight than accuracy.
